Historically low interests rates can have a significant impact on the real-estate market. One of the main ways that low rates influence housing prices is by lowering the cost of borrowing money for homeowners and potential homebuyers. This, in turn, can lead to increased demand for homes, which can push up prices. Here's how it works:
Lower Interest Rates = Lower Monthly Mortgage Payments When interest rate are lower, borrowers can obtain loans with more affordable monthly payments. Because mortgage payments are a large portion of most homeowners' monthly expenses, this can make owning a home more economically feasible for a greater number of people. As a result, there is increased competition for available properties, driving up housing costs.
Low Rates Can Increase Appreciation In addition to influencing the price of homes currently on market, historically-low interest may also contribute to appreciation in housing values over time. When people can afford larger homes or more expensive neighborhoods due to lower mortgage costs, they often choose to buy in these areas. If demand exceeds supply, prices can rise—especially in regions where economic growth and population increase support rising housing demand. Over time, as houses in desirable areas appreciate in value, owners may decide to sell and reinvest the gains in even more costly homes. In some cases, low-interest rates could therefore contribute not only to current housing inflation but also to higher long-term housing value trends.

by John L. Waters III | 2018-05-24 | Leave a comment As a business owner, you might consider hiring freelance workers to help your company grow. However, there are certain tax implications associated with this type of employment that you should be aware of. Here’s what you need to know about hiring freelances and the taxes you may have to pay:
Determine the worker’ s status Before bringing on any new hires, it’ is crucial to determine whether they will be classified as an employee or independent contractor. In the United States, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has set forth guidelines for determining employee versus independent contract status. If the individual meets the criteria for being an independent consultant, then you won’t have any payroll tax responsibilities. But if the person qualifies as your employee, not only will you have payroll taxes obligations but also potential unemployment insurance liabilities and workers compensation coverage.
Withhold and pay payroll and income taxes for employees If you decide to hire someone as a W-9 employee and provide them with a Form W–2 at the end of the year, as required by law, your payroll department must withhold federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare taxes from their paychecks. You’ll also be responsible for paying the employer’ share of these taxes, which typically amounts to approximately 7.65% of an individual’ salary. It’ also essential to ensure that state and local payroll withholding and tax requirements are met in accordance with applicable regulations. The failure to do so could result in penalties and interest charges. Make sure to consult with an accountant or tax professional to understand all applicable state tax rules. They can walk you through how to comply with different state laws. This helps avoid confusion and costly mistakes. For example, California has its own state payroll filing requirements. Moreover, cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco impose their own payroll reporting requirements on employers. So, consult a CPA to make sure you’re compliant with all relevant regulations in each jurisdiction where your business operates. Keep accurate records Regardless of whether you employ an Independent Contractor or an Employee, keeping accurate time records is critical. These records include hours worked, wages paid, deductions made, etc. Accurate records help you calculate and report income and payroll information accurately. Additionally, maintaining complete records ensures compliance with IRS and state labor department regulations, helping prevent audits and other potential issues down the road. Independent contractors don’ t require much record-keeping compared to employees. Maintaining records such as time sheets, invoices, emails discussing work scope, project completion dates, payment history, benefit contributions, or lack thereof, can help protect both parties in case of a dispute. File correct tax returns At the close of every fiscal year and before the deadline, file appropriate federal, state, local,and foreign tax filings for both employees and independent contractors. Always double check tax forms and documentation submitted because errors may lead to delays, fines, interest or even disallowance of credits. Employers who fail to submit timely and accurate payroll reports, withheld taxes or unemployment contributions may face significant penalties from the IRS or other regulatory bodies. Consult an expert While many aspects of freelancing and dealing with taxes are straightforward, others can be complex and confusing. Hiring an experienced accountant, especially one specializing in small business taxation, may prove invaluable in navigating the nuances of employing freelancer and complying with various tax laws across jurisdictions. A qualified tax pro can offer guidance on everything from independent contracting agreements to tax credit opportunities available for employers and employees alike. Staying informed and proactive when it comes to hiring independent workers and managing their taxes can significantly reduce your risk of financial penalties while boosting overall efficiency and productivity within your organization.

If you want to maximize your return on investment (ROI), stocks and high- yield bonds are both viable options but each has its own set of risks and rewards. Here's a look at the risk-reward profile of stocks versus high yielding bonds, as well as potential tax implications of investing in either asset class.
The Risk Profile Stoc k s Investing in stocks involves a higher degree of risk than investing bonds or cash equivalents. Stocks can be volatile, with prices rising and falling rapidly based on market sentiment, economic conditions and company performance. The return from stocks is generally higher than that of bonds and cash, but it also carries the highest probability of losing money if the investment is not managed properly. For risk averse investors, stocks may not be their first choice. However, they remain an essential component of most investment portfolios because of their potential for long-term growth. Stock investors should consider diversification by investing across different industries and geographies to mitigate risk. Diversification does not guarantee profits or protect against losses. It is a method used to help balance investments and reduce risk exposure. Learn more about stock trading risks here. Bonds High-Yield Bonds invest in debt securities issued by companies or governments with below-average credit ratings. They offer a relatively high level of income compared to other fixed-income investments, such as treasuries or investment grade corporate bonds. These securities typically carry a greater risk of default than their higher rated counterparts, which means there is an increased likelihood of the issuer failing to make interest payments or repay the principal amount invested. Investors who choose to allocate capital to high Yield bonds should understand the additional risk involved and ensure that these securities represent a small percentage of total portfolio assets. Read our article on high yielder bond risks for more information. Tax Implications When it comes to taxes, the type of investment you hold will determine how your returns are taxed. Both stocksandhigh-yieldbondsgenerally provide qualified dividend income,whichis taxed at your marginal tax rate. That means the tax burden placed on this income depends on your overall tax bracket. But there are situations where tax strategies can impact your investment decisions. If you have a favorable tax situation, say being in a lower tax brackets or eligible for certain tax credits, then considering investing some of your capital in high dividend paying stocks or bonds could make sense. On the flip side, if you expect your tax liability to increase in the near future, you might prefer to focus on assets with lower dividend yields like real estate or alternative investments. Regardless of what tax strategy you decide to pursue, always consult with a tax professional before implementing any significant changes to your investments or financial plan. Conclusion In summary, when comparing stocks vs high yield bonds for maximizing ROI, each asset offers unique advantages and disadvantages in terms of reward potential and risk profile. Before making an investment decision, consider your risk tolerance, portfolio goals and personal circumstances. Additionally, don't overlook the potential impact of taxes on the overall value of an asset to you. By understanding the risks, rewards, and tax considerations associated with each investment category,youcanmake more informed decisions and better align your portfolio with your financial objectives.

Currency risk is a significant factor for investors when it comes to international portfolios. Here's how to mitigate the impact of currency fluctuations on your investments.
By: Drew Adamek 10/25/19 International investing can offer diversification and growth potential, but it also exposes you to currency risks. Currency risk occurs when the value of one country’s currency depreciates or appreciates compared to another country' s currency. This can impact the returns on investments denominated in a foreign currency, particularly if you hold assets for an extended period. To manage this risk effectively, consider these strategies:
Diversify currencies When investing internationally, try to spread your investment across different currencies. Diversifying currencies helps mitigate exposure to any single currency' fluctuation. By including multiple currencies in your portfolio, you can balance out any losses from one currency with gains in others. Consider investing in stocks, bonds, or funds that have exposure across several countries and currencies, such as global or regional mutual funds or exchange-traded funds (ETFs). These products may allow you access to a broad range of currencies without having to trade individually in each market. ■
Use forward contracts Forward contracts are agreements to buy or sell a currency at a specific rate in the future. They allow investors to lock in current exchange rates, which can help protect against currency volatility. For example, if an investor believes the U.S. dollar will weaken against the euro in six months, they can enter into a forward contract to sell dollars for euros at today' rate. If the dollar does weaken, the investor will profit from the higher euro amount they received when they eventually convert the dollars back to euros. Conversely, should the USD strengthen against EUR,the investor would lose money when converting the EUR back into USD. However, since the forward rate was locked in at the time of the contract, there would be no further loss due to changes in currency values. Use of forward currency contracts requires some knowledge of foreign exchange markets and can be expensive depending on the size of transaction and length of contract. Also, because these contracts involve commitment and future transactions, liquidation or early termination could result in significant costs. So, consult with a professional financial advisor before entering into any forward foreign contract agreement. Invest in companies that generate revenue in multiple geographies Investing in businesses that derive a portion of their revenue from outside their home country can reduce currency exposure relative to their domestic operations. When a company generates sales in several different countries, its revenue isn't quite as exposed to the movement of individual currencies versus the US Dollar. Moreover, selecting firms with diverse global revenue streams can also provide other benefits, like increased product demand, more stable pricing power, and less reliance on a single market or economy. Monitor currency trends regularly Keep a close eye on currency movements and developments in foreign economies. Monitoring the foreign exchanges can give you insights into potential currency swings and inform your decisions about when to reallocate or rebalance your international portfolio. Tracking economic indicators, political events, central bank announcements, interest rate changes, inflation rates and supply-and-demand dynamics are essential factors affecting currencies and should be factored into your decision making process. Seek expert advice While managing currency exposures and mitigating risks can become more complex than simply buying and holding stocks and bonds domestically, seeking guidance from a competent financial adviser can significantly enhance your ability to navigate these challenges successfully. An experienced financial consultant understands the nuances of international markets, currency impacts, tax considerations, asset allocation, risk management techniques, investment vehicles, regulatory compliance and other factors impacting your overall financial plan. In the financial system, two entities create money: central banks and commercial. Although both institutions have different functions, they play a critical role in the creation of currency and credit. Let’s understand their roles and how they create this money.
What is a Central Bank?
A central bank is an organization responsible for managing a country's monetary policy. It controls the currency, money supply, and interest rates in its jurisdiction. The primary objective of a central banking institution is to maintain price stability while achieving economic growth. Some examples of central bankers are the Federal Reserve System (United States), Bank of England (England), European Central Banks (Europe), and the Reserve Bank Of India (India). Many countries have only one central banker, but some like Canada and Australia have more than one. Central bankers also serve as the lender of last resort during financial crises. They provide emergency funding to solvent but temporarily illiquid financial institutions. Thus, ensuring financial stability. In short, a centralized banker is responsible not only for creating money but also controlling it within the economy. 
Central banks can create two types of money; physical currency (coins and notes) and deposit money (reserve accounts at the central broker) that commercial bankers can access to make loans and credits. When a commercial bank extends a loan to a customer, it debits the borrower' s account and crediting the bank 's reserve account at a unified banker. This increases the amount of deposit funds available to the commercial banker to lend out again. So, in this way, unified bankers indirectly create deposit cash that gets circulated throughout the whole economy by commercial lenders. By: John Matarese Posted at 10:13 AM, May 30, 2017 If you've ever paid too much for a vehicle or had a high interest rate loan, you know it can be frustrating. But there are things you can do if you find yourself in that situation.
Jim has a $400 a month car payment on a 72-month loan. His payments total nearly $32,080 over the life of the loan – but his car is only worth $25,905. That means he will spend nearly as much as the car was worth, just to own it!
That's an upside down loan and a lot of money wasted. What can Jim do about it? Not much, unless he wants to put more money into the vehicle. Here are some options:
Pay extra each month until loan is paid off: If you have a few years left on your loan term, continue making payments as usual. Just add an extra $60 or so a Month until your vehicle is worth what you owe on it. This will free up some cash, but could take several years. And it doesn't help with the interest you already paid. Share buyback is a strategy employed by companies to reduce their outstanding share capital and increase the value of remaining shares. It involves a company repurchasing its own shares from investors on the open market. This process can be done through a tender offer, where shareholders are asked to sell their shares at a specified price, or through regular purchases made on exchanges.
Here's how a share repurchase works:
A company decides that it wants to decrease its outstanding shares, which may be motivated by improving earnings per share (EPS), enhancing shareholder value, financing a growth initiative, etc. The board of directors authorizes a repatriation program. After the authorization, the company sets aside the necessary funds for the purchase. These funds can come from retained profits, debt, issuing new shares (known as a 'share issue'), or a combination of these methods. A company typically uses retained earnings or debt to fund share buys back. Some firms use a mixture of cash and debt; this is known as "manufactured liquidity."
The company announces its intention to buy back shares to the public via press releases or filings with regulatory agencies. Companies must disclose the number of shares bought, purchase prices, and the total amount spent under SEC guidelines. Share repricings are usually disclosed in a 8-K filing, while larger repricing plans are disclosed through Form 13D/a filings. Investors who wish to learn about share purchases can look at these documents for more information. Additionally, companies frequently update their investors about their repacement plans during quarterly earnings calls.

The at-the-money leg is usually settled close to expiration, while the out-of- the- money leg settles further out in time.

This is done since the risk profile of these positions can be quite different between the legs, with the OTM leg being more sensitive to changes in volatility expectations than the ATM leg. When you are looking at selling your vehicle and buying a new one, it may be possible to use the proceeds from selling the old car towards part or all of the cost of your new car. This is known as an "upside down" trade in or financed lease turn in. It allows you to get more value out of what you would have otherwise just thrown away by trading it in on a newer model. In this case, you will be financing the new vehicle with the amount you save from not having to pay full price for it. Let's walk through how you can calculate the loss when doing an Upside Down Trade-In.
First, determine the total cash value of both vehicles: The amount that you receive for your traded-off vehicle (the one you sell) must equal the purchase price of their new ride. If you owe money on your current vehicle, its value is less than its purchase value, so youll need to come up with some additional funds to cover the difference. You can estimate the trade value by using Kelly Blue Book or NADA Guides to find a fair market value estimation. Just remember that these estimates are only guidelines and are often subject to negotiation. Its important to know what kind of shape your car is in and how much wear and tear it has endured during its life. A badly damaged car will naturally command a lower price than a well-maintained one. And if your trade has a lot of miles on it, thats another factor that could reduce its resale value. Once youve determined the estimated trade values for both cars, subtract the lesser amount from the greater amount to arrive at the net amount of cash available for the deal. Then divide that number by the sales price (purchase price minus any discount or dealer incentives applied) of whatever vehicle youre buying. That will give you the percentage of savings that comes from trading in the other vehicle. However, keep in mind that the dealer might add a little something extra onto the sticker price to help make the numbers work financially for them. They might also ask for a slightly higher trade allowance than they actually need in order to have some wiggle room to negotiate the final sale price. To figure out how close together these numbers should be, consider asking friends who have recently purchased vehicles and have had similar deals done to see what sort of percentages they received. The best way to ensure you get a good deal is to shop around and compare offers. Dealers often compete against each other for business, particularly on popular models. Ask at several locations before choosing one to do business with. Keep in your mind however, that dealers might try to lowball you on the value you place on trading vehicles. Dont let them take advantage of you! Do your research and hold your ground when negotiating. Remember that its always better to ask questions rather than simply accept the first offer you hear. Finally, be sure to understand exactly what terms and conditions are involved with taking out a loan to finance the balance of purchasing the vehicle being traded in for. "Annual": This refers to the frequency with which the "concurrent retract privilege" can be exercised. In this case, once a year. The shareholder could only exercise this right once every twelve months. This part of the preferred shares might give the shareholder the opportunity to sell their shares back to company at a predefined price or value. “Concurrent Retract Privilage”: This term likely refers either to a "retraction right" or a 'call right', depending on the context of how it' s being used. Here are what those terms mean:
Retraction Right: This is a provision in a security contract allowing one party (usually the issuer/company) to buy back securities from another party after they have already been issued. Usually, these rights come with an established price, called a ‘retention price’. Retractions are often done as a means to re-use the funds from the sold securities. Companies will usually use them if they want to raise capital without incurring permanent debt or issue new shares to purchase assets or cover expenses. For preferred stockholders, having a retractions right gives them flexibility to exit investments if necessary. Some companies may even issue convertible preferred stocks alongside retracions rights to enable investors to convert their preferred stakes into common stock if conditions warrant doing so. If the market value rises above the retention price during the period when the retriction right can exercised then the preference holder may decide not to exercise the right and instead hold onto their investment. 
Call Right : A call right allows one entity (typically the holder of a bond or preferred stake) the option to require another entity to redeem (buy back) its debt, preferred equity, or other security at par value before its due date. They are typically used by companies looking to avoid interest payments or dividend payments, but can also be used to fund new projects or acquisitions. Callable bonds or debentures are securities that contain a call feature where the lender can choose to have their loan repaid before maturity. Similarly, callable preferreds allow holders to demand repayment before the normal expiration date, usually at or near par. 
A "preferred share Annual Concurrent Retriction Privlege" would essentially grant preferred shareholders the ability to withdraw their holdings once per year, most likely for a pre-determined price. How much control or flexibility this gives the shareholders would vary based on specific circumstances like market conditions and company strategy. Ultimately, such clauses provide investors with more options and flexibility than non-callable securities while still offering stability and protection compared to common stocks.

How to Value Pensions Pensions are complex financial instruments, and determining their value requires consideration of several factors. This article will provide an overview of how to value pensions in monetary terms.
What is a Pension?: A pension is an income stream paid by an employer or government entity to an employee after they have stopped working. These payments can continue for the rest of the employee's life or for a specific period of time. Paternal typically consists of a combination of retirement savings, social security benefits, employer contributions, investment returns, interest earnings, etc. It is important to note that not all pensions are equal; some may be more valuable than others depending on various factors such as the size of payments, duration, potential rate of return, risks involved, tax implications, among other things. Determine the type of pension: There are different types of paternal plans including defined benefit plans (e.g., traditional pensions), defined contribution plans, cash balance plans and hybrid plans. Each plan has its unique features and valuation methods which need to be considered separately. For example, defined-benefit plans are based on years of service and final salary while defined contributions plans depend on individual savings and investments. Therefore, it is crucial to identify the exact nature of your pension plan before proceeding further. 
Calculate the present value: To determine a pensions value, you first need calculate its present worth. Present value represents the total amount of money available now if all future payments were converted into their current equivalent using discount rates (usually market rates of interest). Discounting future cash flows helps account for time value and risk. Different discounting techniques may apply depending upon the specifics of each plan. Commonly used methods include the Net Present Value (NPV), the Present Amortized Value, the Livernash Method, or the Modified Duration Analysis. This loss equals the difference between the strike price and the market price at the time you choose to buy the underlying asset (or accept delivery of the asset).
If you hold an in-the-money put, meaning the current market value is below the strikethrough price, then you could exercise your option and lock in your profit by buying the stock at a lower price than it currently trades for. However, if the price rises above the striking price before you have the opportunity to sell or take delivery, you will lose any additional profits that would have been made had you held the shares directly rather than the put. In other words, holding an active put position doesnt protect you from price increases; it merely limits your potential loss.

A: A short sell occurs when an investor borrows a stock they do not own, and sells it. If the stock price drops, the investor can buy it back at the lower price and keep the difference as profit. However, if the price rises, they need to buy the shares at a higher price than they sold them for (because they don't actually own any), resulting in a loss.

These could include property tax, homeowners insurance, maintenance fees, utilities, mortgage interest, depreciation, or anything else related to housing.Documenting these expenditures carefully and accurately will add weight to your claim of economic stress.Be prepared to contribute additional assets or cash.While including an unencumbered asset demonstrates financial commitment, the fact that it’s underwater suggests that additional funding may be needed to bring it back into the black. in a company - taxation and accounting By S V Krishnan, Chartered Accountant (India)
Tax treatment of share capital in India: Tax on shares or equity holdings is governed by various laws and regulations, primarily the Income Tax Act 1961. There are two types of income that arises from shareholding: Long-term capital gains tax and short- term capital gain tax. Long term holds an investment for more than one year whereas short term is holding for less than a year. The rate of tax varies depending upon the period for which the investments were held.
Capital gains arising out of sale of securities (shares/debentures etc.) would be chargeable to tax under the head "Capital Gains" as per the provisions of Income-tax Act, 2017. If the asset is held for over one-year period it is considered as long term asset and taxed at the rate specified in the relevant Schedule to the Act. For assets held between six months to one years it will be treated as short terms asset & taxed with indexation benefit at 45% if the investor has not availed any exemption under section 54EC or 88CCE. In case the capital asset being sold is a residential house property then the same shall be subjected to stamp duty as well as the applicable VAT/CST. However, in case of listed shares, long-terms capital losses can be set off only against long terms capital profits while short term losses may be adjusted against short term profit. Section 72A of the IT act allows for set-off of losses within the block of companies. This implies that both long and Short-Term Capital Losses can only be offset against the corresponding profits of any company within a group of compaines. Thus, capital loss cannot be carried forward indefinitely but must be utilised within five assessment years. Therefore, shareholders should keep track of their holdings so that they do not end up paying tax on unrealized gains. Additionally, foreign investors need to comply with FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act), 03 legislation that governs investment by non-residents in Indian securities. While this article provides an overview of taxes related to shareholdings, it does not constitute legal advice; consult an attorney or qualified accountant before making financial decisions.

Qualified buyers are investors or companies who meet specific criteria established by a company to invest in its stock. In the context of spin-offs, qualified buyers may be required to meet certain requirements when exercising stock option or rights because they have access to information and resources that other investors do not. This is designed to ensure that the company is being acquired by an investor who understands the risks and opportunities associated with the business, and can contribute to its long-term success.
Some reasons why qualified buyer status may apply to stock offerings spun-off from a parent corporation include:
Financial stability: Qualified investors are typically required by law to prove that they possess sufficient financial resources to support their investment and minimize the risk of them becoming insolvent if the investment does not perform as expected. Spin- offs often involve a significant investment of capital, so it’s crucial to make sure potential investors can afford to take on this risk. By requiring qualified investors to demonstrate their financial stability, companies can ensure they are acquiring funds from reliable sources. 
Knowledge and expertise: Investors who qualify as buyers must also demonstrate an understanding of the industry and the specific company they wish to acquire shares in. They should be able to provide evidence of their knowledge and experience through previous investments or relevant work history. Requiring qualified purchasers to show expertise helps ensure the acquisition process is smooth and successful, as well as minimizing the likelihood of misunderstandings or conflicts down the line. It also indicates that these investors will be better equipped to add value to the new company. Corporate governance: Certain investors may want to gain a greater role in the management of a spinoff company than simply investing in their stock and sitting on the board. To prevent this situation, qualifying buyers might need to comply with additional requirements related to corporate governance. For instance, they might have to agree to certain restrictions on their involvement in decision-making processes or commit to specific time commitments. Protecting minority shareholders: Spinoff transactions sometimes involve creating a new publicly traded company from an existing division or subsidiary of another company, which means there will likely be minority shareholde rs present alongside the majority shareholder (the parent). Ensuring that qualified buy ers are invested in a legitimate manner protects the interests of all shareholders, including those with smaller holdings. Transparency: When conducting a public offering, it's essential to maintain transparency throughout the process. Qualifying buyers who participate in spinoffs may need additional documentation or due diligence checks conducted to verify their qualifications and ensure compliance with securities laws. Index Funds are mutual funds that try to match the performance of a particular market index such as S&P 500 or the Dow Jones Industrial Average. They do this by investing in all (or most) of the securities that make up that index in proportion to their weighting. The price of an index fund is determined by the value of its holdings, which is based on the current market price for each security in the index. Therefore, the price will fluctuate throughout the day as the market moves up and down.
The net asset value (NAV) is the calculated value per share of all the assets held by an investment fund. This includes both the funds investments and any cash reserves. Index funds update their NAVs multiple times per day, usually at the close of trading in each market. If youre interested in buying or selling shares in an Index Fund, you can do so at this NAV price. However, if you want to track the total return of your investment over time, its important to focus on this figure rather than the daily price fluctuations.

How After Hours Trading Works After-hours trading refers to transactions that take place outside of regular market hours. While most exchanges around the world close for at least one hour each day, traders still have access to markets through electronic communication networks (ECNs) and dark pools. Dark pools are private trading platforms where large institutional investors and high-frequency traders conduct their trades anonymously. ECNs, on the other hand, are global computer networks that allow traders to communicate and execute trades in real time. When trades occur during after-hour sessions, they are usually reported first by these platforms. Later in some cases, the exchanges themselves will report the transactions. As a result, after hour trading data might not be available until the next day due to reporting delays. After-Hours SDPR: What Is It?
An afterhours SDR is any security represented by an SPR portfolio that is not part of its primary benchmark index but is added to enhance diversification. For example, if an investor owns an SPY which tracks large cap U,S stocks, he could purchase additional aftermarket securities that are not included as part SP 40’S benchmark but could enhance his investment strategy. An aftermarkets security would typically have lower volatility than its underlying benchmark and could add stability to the overall portfolio. Why Are After Hour Stocks Important? In general, there are two main reasons why afterhour trading is important: liquidity and price discovery. Liquidity is essential because it allows investors to buy and sell securities when they need to, without affecting prices significantly. During normal market days, liquidity tends to be higher since more people are actively trading. However, during periods when markets are closed, such as weekends or holidays, or during extended hours, finding buyers or sellers becomes more challenging. Price discovery is crucial because traders use afterhrs trades to determine fair values for securities. Since markets aren’t open, prices for individual stocks or indexes aren t updated constantly like they would be during regular trading hours and traders must rely on other means to assess values. Generally speaking, dark pool and Ecn trading increases the availability of liquidity information during these periods, allowing traders make informed decisions about what prices to offer for specific securities or how much they re willing pay for them.

Market conditions Stock markets generally move up and down based on economic indicators such as interest rates and unemployment. Additionally, market volatility sometimes results in so called option backdating scandals, where companies are accused of manipulating options grant dates in order to benefit certain insiders or management. Bonds rated BBB- or below by S& P or Ba- (or lower) by Moody's are generally considered junk or high yield bonds (although there can be some variance between the two agencies) . Issuers with low ratings typically must pay higher interest rates to attract investors, resulting in higher yields for those willing to take on the additional risk.

If there's more demand than supply, the stock price goes up; if there’s less demand, it goes down. That said, here are some of the factors that contribute to upward and downward pressure on a stock' price:
Fundamental factors affect the intrinsic value of any given security and include things like: earnings per share (EPS), dividends, book value, revenues, profitability, balance sheet strength, debt levels, growth prospects, and industry trends. A company with strong fundamentals may be expected to do well in the future, which should theoretically drive up the company' s stockprice. The quarterly Earning Report you mentioned is one example of these fundamental factors impacting stock pricing. 
Technical Analysis includes analyzing historical stock quotes to determine patterns or trends that might suggest future price movements. Technical analysts pay attention to things such a moving averages, trend lines, support and resistance levels and candlestick patterns, among others. This form of analysis does not focus on the basic fundamentals of companies, but rather on price action itself. However, just because a pattern appears in a chart doesn't mean that the market will follow it; it only indicates that a potential move exists. In your example, a technical analyst might look at past earnings reports and identify certain patterns after which stock went up or down, giving him/her an idea of what to expect when the next report comes out. Fundamental and technical analysts often complement each other. For instance, even though technical indicators can signal a possible move, fundamental analysts can help decide whether or not to take that trade.

By laying off some employees, it allows those employees who were going to vest in restricted shares to be let go, thus preventing any vestings from occurring until after the acquisition is complete. This in turn ensures that the acquiring company only has to take on the responsibility of the employees they have decided to retain.
However, this practice raises ethical concerns because it could be perceived as using layoffs solely for the purpose of avoiding financial obligations owed to employees. Additionally, if employees believe that they were laid off solely due to the impending acquisition, they might feel betrayed by their former employer and could sue for wrongful termination. It's important for company leadership to weigh the pros and cons of using layoff procedures in these situations carefully.

Inherited IRAs, also called "stretch IRAS," allow a beneficiary to extend the tax-deferred status of their inherited retirement account. Taxes are generally not due until the beneficiary begins making withdrawals from the account, which may be years after the original owner's death. However, there are specific rules for taxes assessed when distributions are made from an InherITED IRA.
Distributions from Inhered IRA The distribution of assets from a traditional or Roth IRA to a designated beneficiary is taxed as follows:
Traditional IRA: The taxable portion of the distribution is based on the life expectancy of beneficiary and is paid over a specified period of time. The amount distributed each year is included in the beneficiaries income for that year and taxed at their marginal tax rate. Any after-tax contributions made by the deceased account owner are not included as part of this taxable distribution. Instead, they are considered a return of principal and are non-Taxable. Distributions must begin within five years of death or the entire account will be taxed immediately. Beneficiaries may choose to have the distributions spread out over their life expectance instead of taking the whole amount at once. This is commonly referred to as the stretch IRA strategy. If the stretched distribution plan is chosen, then only the portion distributed in any given year would be taxable. In all cases, the taxable portions should be reported on Form 1099R, even if no taxes were due. Check with your tax advisor for more information about reporting requirements. 
Roth IRA : Because Roth IRas are funded with after tax dollars, distributions from them are usually Tax free. As long as you have met the five-year holding requirement and one of these conditions (the account owners death, becoming permanently disabled, or reaching age 59 ), qualified distributions will not be subject to federal income tax. It is important to check with a tax professional to determine how state taxes may apply. To ensure the withdrawal is qualified, it needs to be taken according to the rules set forth by your Roth agreement. Generally, your beneficiary will need to take required minimum distributions based upon their own life-expectancy.

Last updated: July 2021 | 9 minutes read In the United Kingdom, it is legal for companies and individuals to earn tax-free interest from their business profit. This guide will explain how to do this safely and legally.
What can I earn?
The UK allows companies to save after-tax profits and invest those profits in various ways, including earning interest. These investments must meet certain criteria to be considered 'permitted' or 'qualified' investments. The interest earned from these permitted investments is not subject to further taxation. Here are some examples of permitted investment:
Pensions such as a private pension scheme or personal pension plan Shares or securities purchasing shares or other securities of a company that pays dividends Bonds buying bonds issued by government or public bodies Business investments funding another business with after tax profits Property investing in real estate, such a property development project or commercial property rental Savings account saving money in a bank account earns interest, but may have limited access to funds Is there any limit to how much I can earn and what taxes do I need to pay? 
There is no limit on the amount you can save and earn qualified interest in the UK. However, if your total annual income exceeds certain thresholds, you may become liable for additional taxes on your savings and/or investment income. You should consult a tax professional to ensure you comply with all applicable tax laws. In general, here are the relevant income threshold amounts for UK taxpayers: 1) basic rate taxpayers (25% tax rate): income over 40,001; 3) higher rate tax payers (45%) income between 50.031 and 61,241 per year; and, 7) additional rate (55%), income above 88,851 annually. It is essential to understand your individual situation and consult an accountant or financial advisor for guidance on tax liabilities and strategies. Read more about UK taxation here. How can i make sure my earnings are safe? To keep your earnings safe, follow these steps: Understand the rules and regulations: Make sure you fully understand which investments qualify as permitted or qualified investments under the law. Consult a lawyer or tax expert if necessary. Maintain accurate records: Keep detailed records of all your business transactions, income, and expenses, as well as your investments and interest payments. Check the accuracy of your accounting software and records regularly to avoid errors. Report accurately: Submit accurate information and report your income and investments correctly to HMRC (Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs), the British tax authority. Pay appropriate taxes: Ensure you are paying the correct amount of tax due on qualifying interest income according to your specific circumstances. Invest carefully: Review potential investment opportunities thoroughly before making a decision. Consider risk, return, liquidity, reputation, track record, management team, legal compliance, potential conflicts of interest etc. When selecting investments, be cautious and consider consulting professionals. Monitor and manage risks: Regularly review your portfolio and adjust your holdings when needed to mitigate risks. Be aware of market conditions and trends, especially if they affect your investment. Engage professionally: If required, seek advice from tax experts, lawyers, financial advisors, or investment managers to assist you with tax planning, investments or managing risks associated with earning qualified interests. Remember, ensuring your safety and legality when earning tax free interest depends on complying with regulatory requirements and maintaining accurate financial records. By taking proactive steps and engaging professionals as needed, your qualified earnings can remain secure and tax compliant.

ROE, or return on equity, is a financial metric that indicates the profitability of a company relative to the value of its shareholders’ equity. It is calculated by dividing net income (profit) by shareholders' equity and expressed as a percentage. The maximum possible ROEs are limited only by the imagination and creativity of company managers – but it is highly unlikely for any real-world company to achieve a true ROA over 50%, much less 70 or 80 percent. Let us see how this could happen.
Theoretically, a return (ROA) on assets in excess of 65% would imply that all profits were coming from asset sales. Assume a bank had $1 million in equity investments and made $2 million selling off some of those investments. That would result in a ROAE of around 201%. But if you think about it, the bank sold some investment portfolios worth $3 million ($2m profit + $0.5m in cash/cash equivalents), so there is no way that a normal bank can have a truly excessive ROEA. In addition, banks must retain a certain amount of capital to be considered well-capitalized according to banking regulations. This means they cannot use all their equity for lending out or investing, which limits what they can earn. While some banks may have high ROAs during bull markets, these are usually temporary phenomena. And they never get close to levels where investors begin to question the validity of reported numbers.

The risk of an early termination of your lease agreement varies depending on the type of property and the terms of the lease. Generally, here are some potential risks:
Lost security deposit: If you break your rental agreement before the end of its term, you may not get back any part or all of what you paid as a security/last month's rent deposit.
Penalties: You might have to pay a penalty for early cancellation, which can be a certain percentage of rent or a set amount. This is often stipulated in the rental contract. The penalty can range from a few months' rent to the entire remaining rental period. It depends on how far in advance you give notice and whether there are any clauses in your tenancy agreement that allow the landlord to charge more. If the tenancies act 1988 allows it, landlords may claim "damages" in addition to any agreed penalties. Punishment amounts can in theory be unlimited (and can sometimes be high). Even if the total claimed is limited by the Act to a maximum of six times the monthly rent, a landlord who is unscrupulous (or knows that collecting unlimited damages would be difficult) can still drive up legal costs. However, these types of damages can only be claimed in very specific circumstances, and landlords will need to show financial loss. Courts are often reluctant to make landlords jump through the hoops when other avenues are open to them (such as claiming a contractual penalty) and will rarely award damages in circumstances where the tenant has vacated the premises but caused no damage. Legal fees incurred by either party (usually the tenants) should be taken into account by a court when considering whether it is worth it to try to claim damages. In practice, the potential for large legal bills is usually enough to discourage landlords from pursuing this route. Unless you have a particularly bad landlord or your local courts tend to lean towards landlords, damages are generally seen as an ineffective way for landlords to recover losses due to early lease termination.

Volatility is a measure of the variability or risk associated with the return on an investment. It is often expressed as a percentage, representing the range of possible returns (or losses) that an investor might experience. Volatile investments have wide swings in their value, while less volatile investments exhibit more stable price movements.
Beta, on the other hand, is an indicator of a security’s or portfolio’ s volatility relative to the market as whole. A beta of 1 means that the security or fund moves in lockstep with its benchmark index; a beta below 0 indicates that it moves less than the benchmark, and a number above 2 suggests that its movements are more extreme than those of its index. In general, a higher beta value implies a greater degree of risk. The relationship between volatility and beta can be described as inverse: as one increases, the others tends to decrease. This means a highly volatile investment will tend to have a low beta, indicating that relative risk is low compared to its performance variation. On the contrary, when volatility is lower, there would be a tendency for betas to increase, suggesting that increased risk may lead to greater price fluctuations.

loan mortgage personal loan Loan Terms Defined A loan is a borrowed amount of money that the borrower must repay with interest. Loan terms define the conditions under which the loan was obtained, including the repayment schedule and any penalties for late payments or defaulting on the agreement.
Here are some common loan terms:
Interest Rate: The cost of the borrowed money, expressed as a percentage or decimal fraction of either the principal amount or the annual equivalent amount. In simple terms, it's how much you have to pay back in addition to the original loan amount in order to borrow the money. The interest rate will affect the total cost and length of your loan. It may also be fixed or variable (floating). Fixed interest rates do not change during the term of a loan, while variable rates can fluctuate based on market conditions. Interest is usually paid either at the beginning of each payment period or added to each monthly payment. Some loans offer interest-only payments for part of their terms followed by balloon payments, where all or a large portion of interest is due at once before the final payment is made. This approach can make it easier to qualify for a larger loan than might otherwise be available. Balloon loans are most commonly used for larger amounts, such as home mortgages or business loans. Amortization: Is the gradual repayment of debt through regular periodic payments. These payments include both principal and interest until the balance is fully repaid. There are several types of amortized loans, like fixed-rate mortgages and car loans; however, there are also non-amortizing loans (also known as balloon loans), such credit cards and some personal loans or lines of credit. Prepayment Penalty: A fee charged if you pay off your debt early or refinance your existing loan before its scheduled maturity date. Such fees are designed to discourage borrowers from paying off their debts too quickly, since they reduce the amount lenders could earn in interest over the full term. Prepayment privileges allow borrowers to refi or payoff their loan whenever they choose without penalty. They come standard on most adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) but may be negotiated into other types. Credit Score: An individual' s credit rating, calculated using a secret formula based primarily on publicly available information about past credit history, debts, and loan payments (late or missed payments carry more weight than just making your payments late) and provided by one or more major credit bureaus. Your credit score impacts your ability to obtain loans and at what interest, particularly when applying for mortgages, car financing, personal or unsecured loans etc. Lenders use credit scores as an indicator of risk when approving loans to determine how likely you are to repay them. When applying, having good credit helps you get approved faster and often at a lower interest level compared to people with poor credit records. APR: Annual Percentage Rate expresses the effective cost for borrowing money annually. Its a more comprehensive measure of costs than simply looking at interest only because it includes other expenses, typically origination fees, points, or processing charges. As a result, the APR can sometimes seem higher than the stated interest alone, even though its still calculated as just a fraction. For instance, if a 15% interest loan has a $300 originations fee and an 8% APR, its actually costing around 23% yearly. Disbursement: Transferring funds to someone else, usually for the purposes of paying for goods or services received. A loan may require disbursea t to be made directly to a third party, rather than to you personally. Collateral: Something of value given up by the person taking out a secured loan to ensure repayment. If the lender should suffer a loss due to nonrepayment, they would then be able to seize upon said collateral to compensate themselves for their losses. Secured Loans involve giving up tangible assets, i.e. cars, homes, boats, RVs, jewelry or art as security. Unsecurred Loans, on other hand, are guaranteed solely by your promise to make repayments. Debt-to-Income Ratio (DTI): Refers to your monthly housing expense relative to gross monthly income. High DTI ratios can indicate a greater risk of default and can impact your eligibility for certain loan products. Mortgage lenders will usually consider anything above 36% to 40% as high risk. Minimum Credit Scores Required: As banks and lending institutions set minimum required credit ratings for different loan types to reduce risk, borrowers who meet these criteria are more likely to receive approval. While credit requirements vary between loan categories, a FICO score of 620 or higher is generally considered satisfactory for most loan applications. Late Fees: Charges imposed on borrowers for missing or being late with loan repaymen ts. Typically, these fines range from a few dollars to several percent of unpaid balances. Borrowers should always read carefully the fine print related to late fees and other relevant fees. Annual Fees/Origination Fees /Points: Cost associated with taking on a new loan or refinancing an existing one. Points are expressions of fee as multiples of one-hundredth of an interest point. Origination costs may include underwriting, document preparation, processing, closing and funding fees among others. Costs can add up to significantly impact overall loan costs. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs): Lists frequently asked questions related specifically to loans in general or to certain types or issues surrounding loans offered by financial institutions. FAQ sections provide useful insights and answers regarding specific loan topics. Trailing twelve- month (TTM) total return is a metric used by investment analysts and financial planners to measure the performance of a mutual fund, stock or other investment vehicle over a specified period of time. It represents the percentage change in the value of an investment from the time it was purchased to the present day, assuming that dividends or distributions have been reinvested back into the investment. The TTM period usually spans twelve months, although it can be any length of period, such as three months or six months.
To calculate trailing twelve month total returned, the following steps are taken:
Calculate the price of the security at the end of each month within the selected time period (usually one year). This involves taking the closing price on the last trading day of every month and adding those prices together. For securities that trade on a daily basis, like stocks, this would involve summing the daily closing prices for each day within that month. Dividend payments or distribution of capital are not included in these prices. If there were no transactions during the month, then the opening price from that previous month is used. Note that if the instrument was not traded for a particular month or had a zero price, it should be excluded from calculations involving that specific month but can still be included when calculating the average price for the entire period. 
Divide the total amount of money invested by the number of shares held at each monthly price point. Doing so gives you the weighted average cost of acquiring shares at that price. In other words, what would the current share price be if all shares had been acquired at exactly that cost? . Calculate a new price today (either the market close or closing bid for non-traded securities), which serves as a base price or "anchor" for our analysis. Subtract the anchor price (today's price) from each of our monthly weighted averages from step #2 to obtain a figure representing the increase or decrease in value since purchase. Then, add those amounts together and divide by 24 (the number or months in a year), giving you a percentage representation of your cumulative total ROI. As with step two, exclude any months where there was no transaction or a price below zero.

A company typically uses retained earnings or debt to fund share buys back. Some firms use a mixture of cash and debt; this is known as "manufactured liquidity."
The company announces its intention to buy back shares to the public via press releases or filings with regulatory agencies. Share repricings are usually disclosed in a 8-K filing, while larger repricing plans are disclosed through Form 13D/a filings. A contract for difference (CFD) is an over-the-counter derivatives trading instrument. It allows investors to speculate on price movements of assets like stocks, commodities, indices and currencies without actually owning them. CFDs are traded on a margin basis, which means that traders only need to deposit a fraction of the total value of their position in order to open a trade. This article will explain how a typical CFd works behind- the-scenes.
Opening a Position When a trader wants to buy or sell a particular asset via a contract-for-difference they need first to find a broker willing to take the opposite side of that trade, as well as provide access to the relevant market. The trader sends an order, specifying the desired amount of contracts (usually denominated in lots), the price at which they wish to enter the trade (the ‘strike’ price), and whether they want to go long (buy) or short (sell). Once the broker receives this order it checks availability with its liquidity providers and either accepts or declines the order depending on market conditions and its own risk management policies. If accepted, the trader now has a long or a short position on the asset. For example, if a farmer wanted to protect themselves from a drop in wheat prices by buying a put option, they would open an short CF D position. In contrast, someone who believes that gold prices will rise might open long CFDD position by purchasing a call option. Both these positions have different risks and rewards. A short call position would be opened by selling a gold call. Traders can also close out their existing positions before the expiration date by entering opposite orders. Closing out a position generates a profit or loss based on how much the market moved since opening the position, less any brokerage fees or commissions. When the contract expires, there is no further obligation between the two parties except possibly to settle up any differences between their cash accounts. However, many brokers offer a range of rollover options allowing traders to maintain their positions beyond expiry. These include automatic rolling over, rolling manually or closing out the existing position and re-opening another one at the new strike price. Margin Calls and Maintenance Requirements To manage its counterparty risk, a brokerage firm requires traders who hold open CF DD positions to post collateral known as margin. Depending on an individual trader’s credit-risk assessment, margin requirements may vary significantly. Brokers typically apply maintenance requirements during periods when markets experience significant volatility or sudden moves in prices. Maintenance requirements are designed to ensure that each trader maintains enough available funds or collateral to cover potential losses on their current positions. Should a traders margin fall below their maintenance requirement, brokers may issue a so-called ‘margin call’, requiring additional funds to be deposited immediately to bring the account back into compliance. Failure to do so could result in a termination of your position or even a forced liquidation, potentially leading to large losses. Settlement Settlement occurs when a trades underlying asset reaches the agreed upon strike or expiring price, or when positions are closed out. At settlement time, both the buyer and seller of a futures contract agree to exchange the difference between what the underlying instrument was worth at expiration and the strike/entry price specified in the initial trade – minus any commissions or fees. The at-the-money leg is usually settled close to expiration, while the out-of- the- money leg settles further out in time.

This is done since the risk profile of these positions can be quite different between the legs, with the OTM leg being more sensitive to changes in volatility expectations than the ATM leg. By separating the settlements, counterparties can better manage their risks and minimize the impact of any significant moves in the market during the life of this strategy.

A contract for difference (CFD) is an over-the-counter derivatives trading instrument. It allows investors to speculate on price movements of assets like stocks, commodities, indices and currencies without actually owning them. CFDs are traded on a margin basis, which means that traders only need to deposit a fraction of the total value of their position in order to open a trade. This article will explain how a typical CFd works behind- the-scenes.
Opening a Position When a trader wants to buy or sell a particular asset via a contract-for-difference they need first to find a broker willing to take the opposite side of that trade, as well as provide access to the relevant market. The trader sends an order, specifying the desired amount of contracts (usually denominated in lots), the price at which they wish to enter the trade (the ‘strike’ price), and whether they want to go long (buy) or short (sell). Once the broker receives this order it checks availability with its liquidity providers and either accepts or declines the order depending on market conditions and its own risk management policies. If accepted, the trader now has a long or a short position on the asset. For example, if a farmer wanted to protect themselves from a drop in wheat prices by buying a put option, they would open an short CF D position. In contrast, someone who believes that gold prices will rise might open long CFDD position by purchasing a call option. Both these positions have different risks and rewards. A short call position would be opened by selling a gold call. Traders can also close out their existing positions before the expiration date by entering opposite orders. Closing out a position generates a profit or loss based on how much the market moved since opening the position, less any brokerage fees or commissions. When the contract expires, there is no further obligation between the two parties except possibly to settle up any differences between their cash accounts. However, many brokers offer a range of rollover options allowing traders to maintain their positions beyond expiry. These include automatic rolling over, rolling manually or closing out the existing position and re-opening another one at the new strike price. Margin Calls and Maintenance Requirements To manage its counterparty risk, a brokerage firm requires traders who hold open CF DD positions to post collateral known as margin. Depending on an individual trader’s credit-risk assessment, margin requirements may vary significantly. Brokers typically apply maintenance requirements during periods when markets experience significant volatility or sudden moves in prices. Maintenance requirements are designed to ensure that each trader maintains enough available funds or collateral to cover potential losses on their current positions. Should a traders margin fall below their maintenance requirement, brokers may issue a so-called ‘margin call’, requiring additional funds to be deposited immediately to bring the account back into compliance. Failure to do so could result in a termination of your position or even a forced liquidation, potentially leading to large losses. Settlement Settlement occurs when a trades underlying asset reaches the agreed upon strike or expiring price, or when positions are closed out. At settlement time, both the buyer and seller of a futures contract agree to exchange the difference between what the underlying instrument was worth at expiration and the strike/entry price specified in the initial trade – minus any commissions or fees. By Krishna Natarajan on December 16, 2021 Investing in Indices is one of the most preferred ways of saving money. Both ETF and Mutual Funds have their own pros and cons, but choosing the right one depends upon your investment goals, risk appetite, and financial plan. Lets discuss both these investment vehicles briefly to understand how they work and help you make an informed decision.
Mutual Funds vs ETF What is an Exchange Traded Fund (ETF)? How does it work? An ETF is a security that tracks the performance of a specific index such as S&P BSE Sensex or Nifty 50. It is listed on a stock exchange, just like shares. Investors can buy and sell ETF units anytime during the trading hours through a broker. The price of an ETF unit fluctuates based on the market value of its underlying assets. For instance, if the NIFTY 30 index rises by 05%, then the value or NAV of Nifty 40 ETF will also rise by approximately .04-06% depending on its holdings and expense ratio. So, when you invest, you get exposure to the entire index instead of only a few stocks. This makes it ideal for those who want to diversify their portfolio. But since it trades like a share, there is the potential for capital loss. There is also a cost associated with buying and selling ETF Units called Expense Ratio which varies from fund to fund and is usually around %, depending upon the scheme. Check out the best performing ETF schemes here. Click Here To Know More About ETF Investment Options Now, lets dive into what is Mutual funds? A mutual fund is managed by a fund manager who invests in stocks, bonds, or other assets according to a pre-defined investment strategy. These funds are divided into categories such a Equity Fund, Debt Fund or Balanced Fund depending upn the investment approach. A debt fund typically invests more than 60% of it assets in debt instruments like bonds while an equity fund has more investments in equities. Some funds even allow you to customise your portfolio like SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) where you can invest a fixed amount at regular intervals. Mutual fund prices are calculated once a day (usually at the end of each business day) based upon its net asset value (NAV), which is determined by the total value less liabilities of all the securities held by them. Risk Appetite: If you have a low tolerance for risk and wish to maintain stability in your returns, a mutual may be a better option as it provides diversification and stability. However, in case you are willing to take higher risks for higher rewards, an EFT could be suitable. They offer exposure only to selected indices and thus carry higher volatility. Keep in mind that high volatility does not necessarily imply losses; it simply means the price can fluctuate significantly. Since ETF prices change throughout the day, traders can lock in profits or reduce losses by timing their trades well. Whereas Mutualfunds are priced once per day after the close of market. Hence, timing becomes comparatively harder. Take a look at our mutualfund return calculator to check historical returns before making any decisions. Calculate MutualFund Returns Transaction costs: Trading ETF involves transaction costs similar to that of stock transactions including brokerage fees. While buying or selling mutual units, transaction charges include application fee, exit load, etc. Depending on your trade size, these expenses can add up. Thus, compare the expense ratios and transaction fees carefully before investing. Find Out How Much Does An Sip Cost Tax efficiency: ETF gains are taxed as per the tax slab you fall under while mutual gains depend on whether you hold the unit for more or less than a year. Long term investors can save taxes by investing through ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme) which offers tax benefits under Section 80C of Income Tax Act. Therefore, understanding the taxation aspect helps efficiently allocate your resources. Learn How EL SS Helps Save Taxes Liquidity: Both ETFS and MFs offer good liquidity. Evaluate Liquidity Before Investing Diversification: With ETF, your entire investment goes towards the index you choose and offers diversified exposure. Explore Diversified Mutual Schemes For Risk Averse Investors Cost efficiency and convenience: Typically, ETF are cheaper than mutual especially when it comes to transaction cost. Analyse Your Financial Goals And Compare Costs In conclusion, selecting an ETF or mutual for index investing boils down to evaluating your risk tolerance, investment objectives, time horizon, taxation benefits, costs, tracking accuracy, liquidity, diversification, personal preference, financial knowledge, maintenance and monitoring. What is Discount Rate? Discount rate is a percentage used as a discounting factor when calculating the present value (PV) of future cash flows. It reflects the investor’ s required rate for capital, which represents the cost of capital or the minimum rate that investors need to earn on their investment in order to invest. Discount rates can vary depending on the risk associated with an asset, its expected life span, and market conditions. In other words, it is the rate at which you would be willing to pay today for a payment received in the future. The higher the discount rates, the lower the PV of the cash flow, reflecting the fact that you require more money now to receive less money later. Volatility is a measure of the variability or risk associated with the return on an investment. It is often expressed as a percentage, representing the range of possible returns (or losses) that an investor might experience. Volatile investments have wide swings in their value, while less volatile investments exhibit more stable price movements.
Beta, on the other hand, is an indicator of a security’s or portfolio’ s volatility relative to the market as whole. A beta of 1 means that the security or fund moves in lockstep with its benchmark index; a beta below 0 indicates that it moves less than the benchmark, and a number above 2 suggests that its movements are more extreme than those of its index. In general, a higher beta value implies a greater degree of risk. The relationship between volatility and beta can be described as inverse: as one increases, the others tends to decrease. This means a highly volatile investment will tend to have a low beta, indicating that relative risk is low compared to its performance variation. On the contrary, when volatility is lower, there would be a tendency for betas to increase, suggesting that increased risk may lead to greater price fluctuations.

The question of where to classify cryptocurrencies is a complex one. Cryptocurrencies are not traditional currencies, nor can they be categorized solely as commodities or securities. They have characteristics of each of these categories and also possess unique features that set them apart from all three.
There are several ways to consider categorizing cryptocurrencies:
Commodity - Cryptocurrency can be classified as a commodity if it is viewed as an alternative to gold or other precious metals. However, this classification does not fully capture the complex nature of cryptocurrency; commodities do not typically have the same decentralized, digital, or borderless qualities as cryptocurrencies. Additionally, many cryptocurrencies are designed to be more than just a store of value, making the commodity category insufficient.
Security Äì Some cryptocurrencies, such as Bitcoin, are often referred to as securities because their value depends on the performance of an underlying company or project. In the case of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies with a limited supply, price appreciation is primarily driven by demand and supply factors rather than underlying performance. This distinction makes it difficult to place all cryptocurrencies in the security category. Moreover, security regulations vary significantly between countries and regions, which would make it challenging to create a universal framework for regulating cryptocurrencies as such. Therefore, calling cryptocurrencies Ô¨Ånancial instruments (securities) may not be accurate enough either. UK GilTS, or UK Government Index-Linked Bonds, are a type of fixed-income investment that provides protection against inflation. They are issued by the UK government to raise money for various purposes, such as funding public services and reducing the deficit. UK gilts are debt securities, which means they represent a claim on the government’s future income or tax receipts. Investors buy gilt bonds in order to receive regular interest payments (coupons) and a final repayment of the principal amount upon maturity.
The interest rate on a gild is usually set at a fixed rate for the entire term of its issuance, often between one and 30 years. This means that the investor will receive the same coupon payment each year throughout the life of their investment. Interest payments are made semiannually, usually on June 5 and December 6 each years, and are paid out of tax revenues collected by HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). The interest is taxable as ordinary income in the year it is received. Some gilmets also include a link to an index, typically the Retail Prices Index (RPI), which can result in inflation-linked adjustments to the coupon payments. If the RPI increases, so too will the coupons paid on those gils. Conversely, if the index decreases, the payments will be reduced accordingly. However, many gilsts have become "index-unlinked" in recent years with inflation protection provided through other means, e.g., TILTs (Index-linking through the yield) or through equities. But the core problem is not so much these countries as it is the euro itself and the two-tier financial system upon which it rests. Germany, Austria, Finland, Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg are the countries that use the single currency; they have a fractional reserve banking system called the TARGET2 settlement system. A fraction reserve bank can create money out of thin air by lending more than its capital base. In a crisis, the fractionally-reserve bank calls in loans, destroying the extra money it created, causing a contraction of credit and a deflationary spiral. This is how the United States collapsed into the Great Depression after the 9/11 attack, when banks called in their loans and stopped making new ones. There are several reasons why a credit-card issuer might consider waiving an annual fee, including:
Customer service: Banks and credit unions often want to retain loyal customers. As a way to show appreciation for your business, they may waived the fee. This tactic is especially common with high-yield or rewards cards.
Promotional offer: Credit card issuers sometimes run promotions offering new customers a waiver of the first annual membership fee or introductory APR. You can usually find these offers on the bank's website or in promotional materials. Make sure to read the fine print to understand any restrictions or expiration dates. 
Lack of competition: If you have a low interest rate or no-fee options from other banks, it might encourage your current issuber to waives its annual fees. Consider shopping around for better deals before asking for a fee waiver. Also, if you plan on using the card infrequently or for low-dollar purchases, there'll be little incentive for the company to keep charging you. Some issuars may also waivers fees as long as you meet certain spending requirements each month or year. These "inactivity" fees are designed to encourage users to spend more money so that the issur can make more revenue off of them. However, some companies may choose to forego the fees altogether rather than risk alienating their customer base by charging something they feel isn't necessary. In all cases, contacting the issuing bank or credit union directly should produce the most accurate information about whether or not they're willing to forgive your annual card fees; however, a few general guidelines can help guide you toward understanding when and why such actions might take place.

If you have a positive Delta, meaning that your position moves in the same direction as the underlying asset, then a rise in its price will result in a profit. A high watermark is the highest net asset value (NAV) achieved by a Mutual Fund investment portfolio during its current fiscal year or since the last time the fund paid a performance fee. In other words, it is an internal benchmark for measuring the funds' performance. If the NAV of the mutual funds reaches a high-water mark in a particular period, then it becomes eligible to pay a Performance Fee to the investment manager/advisor.
Performance Fees are charges that are paid to investment managers/ advisors based on the performance of their managed portfolios. The amount of such fees varies depending on how well the portfolios have performed compared to their respective benchmarks. High watermarks act as a barrier for performance-based fees because they ensure that the investments achieve a certain threshold before any additional fees can be paid. This helps protect investors from paying unnecessary fees when the portfolio's performance is not exceptional.
