The order then enters the marketplace and remains pending until the close of trading for that day, at which point it becomes active and is executed. If the prevailing market price matches or is within the predefined price range of their order when trading closes, it will be executed at that price. In cases where the current market rate differs from the specified price, trades may not occur, leaving the trader' s position open until trading resumes the following day or until they manually cancel their market closing order. Some exchanges allow market closure orders to be set up as "fill or kill" orders, meaning that if the order isn't executed by the time the markets close, It will automatically be cancelled. Fill or Kill orders are ideal for traders who need certainty that their orders will execute before the deadline. On the other hand, some exchanges do not support fill or kille orders. When using a fill-or-kill strategy, you should always check with your broker about what is allowed on the exchange you use. When you invest in a call option, you are betting that the stock will rise above the strike price by the time the option expires. If it does not, your investment will lose all of its value and you will not earn any returns. However, if the stocks rises above strike, then you could potentially earn unlimited profits until the options expires because you only risked investing a small amount of capital (the premium you paid for the call). This is similar to a lender earning interest on their loan because they risk nothing more than the principal amount they lent out.
On the other hand, when you buy short stocks, as an investor you can also potentially make unlimited gains if you correctly predict the decline in the share price. In this case, however, there is always some amount that you stand to lose no matter how far the shares fall - this is called your margin liability or maintenance margin. The amount at risk here is the full value of the short position which includes the cost of buying back the borrowed shares at a later date should the market recover. As with a traditional loan, the lender still retains ownership of their collateral even if it increases in value while being lent. Therefore, a mixed strategy combining calls and shorts can be compared to taking on both interest-earning loans and providing collateral to protect against potential losses.

There are various fees associated with the process of buying or selling real estate. These can include commissions, document preparation costs, transfer taxes, inspections, appraisals and more. The specific fees vary by area and transaction type, but here is an overview of what to expect:
Buyer’s Broker Commission: This is typically a one-time fee paid to the realtor representing the buyer. It usually ranges from 2-6% of the sales price, though some states have a mandatory maximum commission.
Seller’ Broker Commision: Similar to a buyer's broker, this is a fee charged by the seller' agent for their services. Typically, the selling agent gets paid from the proceeds of sale, which means that you will not have to pay out of pocket for this fee. However, there may be situations where it is negotiated as part of your listing agreement. This range varies between 3-8%, though again, some areas do have mandated maximums. 
Document Preparation Fees: These fees cover things like title insurance, deed preparation, and recording fees. They can add up to several hundred dollars but are generally relatively small compared to other fees in the transaction. Some realtors may offer to absorb these costs if they are partaking in a large number of transactions at once (known as a "fee split"). In this case, you would not need to worry about paying these fees directly. 
Transfer Taxes: Transfer taxes are levied on the purchase and sale of real property and help fund local government services and infrastructure. Rates vary widely by location, so check with your local tax assessor' office for specific rates applicable to your transaction and jurisdiction. You can often find estimated transfer tax amounts on public records websites or through your realty professional. 
Home Inspection Fee: Home inspections cost anywhere between $300-$150 per hour, depending on your region and the size and scope of work needed. Inspectors review the property' infrastructure, mechanical systems, roof, plumbing, electrical, etc., to ensure everything is functioning properly and safe. Generally, buyers will cover the cost of inspection since it helps them make an informed decision before committing to purchase. 
Appraisal Fee and Credit Check: Lenders require appraisal reports to determine the estimated value of a property for loan purposes. Appraisers typically charge between a few hundred to over a thousand dollars, dependent on property value and appraisal method. Buyers who qualify for a mortgage also undergo a credit check, usually around $40, from a third-party agency to verify their financial history and ability to repay the loan. As a general rule, these expenses are typically borne by prospective homeowners who intend to obtain a loan for the down payment. 
Prepaid Items: Some sellers choose to prepay items such as property taxes or homeowners association dues in order to clear the bill before closing. If you decide to do this, be sure to factor in those costs into your calculations. 
Closing Costs Lawyer Fees, Escrow Fees): These costs can vary depending upon the complexity of each transaction, documentation required, state regulations, escrow company fees, title company charges, survey costs and others. Closing attorneys handle the actual transfer of title and legal paperwork, while escrows manage the funds and disbursements throughout the closing process. Consult with a lawyer or escrowing service for detailed costs applicable in your situation. 
In summary, when purchasing and selling homes, keep in mind that fees can accumulate quickly. Be prepared to budget appropriately for these expected expenses, as well as any surprises that might arise during the course of negotiations and closing processes.

By Investopedia Staff Low-volume trading days, also known as thin trading or light trading, are those in which the number of shares traded is relatively small compared to the total number that are outstanding. This may be due to factors such as holidays, weekends, or periods when investors have little interest in the security. Despite its seeming insignificance, low-volatility trading sessions can sometimes have a significant impact on a company's stock prices. Here're some reasons why:
Market Maker Impact In most stock exchanges, market makers act as intermediaries between buyers and sellers, maintaining a continuous two-way market for a specific security throughout the trading day. They quote bid and ask prices for stocks they intend to buy or sell at any given time, and execute trades at these prices as orders come in. The size of their quotes determines how liquid a security is, with larger quotes providing more liquidity and reducing the impact of individual trades on the stock' price.
When market maker quotes are relatively smaller than average during a low trading volume day, the effect of every trade executed becomes comparatively more significant. As a result, even a few large transactions can cause the price to fluctuate significantly. If such transactions involve a large institutional investor or an influential individual trader, it could lead to a substantial change in a firm' s stock valuation. For instance, if one large shareholder decides to purchase or offload a sizable chunk of stock, this might affect the entire market' value of the company. Moreover, such large trades may trigger further price movements among other traders who are watching the developments closely. In this case, a seemingly inconsequential level of trading activity can lead the share price up or down dramatically. It is worth noting that not all market-makers quote the same size. Some firms may operate with bigger quotes, which means they have more influence on stock pricing; others choose to focus on smaller markets or specific securities. Thus, during low volumes, certain quotes will have greater impact than others, depending on market participants' strategies. Institutional Activity Institutional investors are large entities - such banks, mutual funds, pension funds that manage huge sums of money on behalf of various clients. Their transactions often have much more impact compared with retail investors', since they involve vast amounts of capital. Large institutions like to conduct their trades quietly without attracting too much attention from the market. Low volume periods provide them with such an opportunity. When large institutions are active in buying or selling a particular stock during quiet periods, their activities can easily push the prices upwards or downward. Such movements might not be visible during normal trading conditions, but on low volatility days their impact stands out clearly. Speculation and Rumor Mill Stock markets are known for their propensity to spread rumors and speculation, especially when trading volumes are low. These rumors can make or break companies by altering market sentiment and driving prices up and down. Sometimes, baseless gossip about a corporation' impact its stock value, leading to wild price fluctuations. During light volume days when fewer people are actively trading securities, rumors become more conspicuous and can have significant consequences on share prices, amplifying their effects. Financial News Events Financial news releases, earnings reports, mergers & acquisitions announcements, etc. can heavily influence stock values. On low volumetric days these events can create ripple effects across the board, affecting multiple companies or industries simultaneously. News that may seem insignificant under regular circumstances can produce dramatic changes in stock valuations when volumes drop. Trading Algorithms Algorithmic trading has become increasingly prevalent in recent years, accounting for over half of all trading in equity markets. Many of these algorithms rely on historical data and trends to determine when to initiate a transaction. Due to lower trading levels, historical patterns may appear more meaningful than usual, causing automated trading systems to react strongly to data points that might otherwise have gone unnoticed. Conclusion Although volume is usually viewed as an indicator of market health and liquidity, there are cases where low turnover can still have profound impacts on security prices of a publicly traded entity. With more and more traders relying on electronic networks and algorithmic tools to execute their orders, what used to be considered minor market movement can now have far-reaching consequences. At times, high-profile transactions, institutional activity, rumor mongering, financial news,and algorithm-driven decisions can combine to drive significant fluctuations in share value despite minimal trading. Understanding these dynamics can help investors stay cautious and make informed choices when managing their portfolios.

Short selling involves borrowing a security and then selling it in the hope that its price will fall, allowing you to buy it back at a lower price and return it to the lender. This is different from selling securities to reduce risk exposure or raise cash for other investments. When you sell securities as part of a hedging strategy, you are reducing your exposure to market movements by offsetting gains or losses with an opposite position in another asset. In contrast, when you short sell a stock, your goal is to profit from a decline in its value.
A common example of using securities sales to manage risk is selling a portion of your portfolio, called "selling to cover" or "covered call writing," where you agree to sell shares of stock at some future date at an agreed-upon price (the strike price) and in return receive a premium payment. If the stock's price rises above the strike, the writer of the call option would have to purchase shares to meet the option contract and could either hold them or sell them again if they expected the price to decline. Conversely, if the share price declines below the agreed upon strike value, then the options holder would not exercise their right to be delivered the shares but the seller would keep the premium. Either way, this strategy reduces risk because the holder is only entitled to shares if their price exceeds the designated strike and the author of that option keeps the premiums received.

Currency risk is a significant factor for investors when it comes to international portfolios. Here's how to mitigate the impact of currency fluctuations on your investments.
By: Drew Adamek 10/25/19 International investing can offer diversification and growth potential, but it also exposes you to currency risks. Currency risk occurs when the value of one country’s currency depreciates or appreciates compared to another country' s currency. This can impact the returns on investments denominated in a foreign currency, particularly if you hold assets for an extended period. To manage this risk effectively, consider these strategies:
Diversify currencies When investing internationally, try to spread your investment across different currencies. Diversifying currencies helps mitigate exposure to any single currency' fluctuation. By including multiple currencies in your portfolio, you can balance out any losses from one currency with gains in others. Consider investing in stocks, bonds, or funds that have exposure across several countries and currencies, such as global or regional mutual funds or exchange-traded funds (ETFs). These products may allow you access to a broad range of currencies without having to trade individually in each market. ■
Use forward contracts Forward contracts are agreements to buy or sell a currency at a specific rate in the future. They allow investors to lock in current exchange rates, which can help protect against currency volatility. For example, if an investor believes the U.S. dollar will weaken against the euro in six months, they can enter into a forward contract to sell dollars for euros at today' rate. If the dollar does weaken, the investor will profit from the higher euro amount they received when they eventually convert the dollars back to euros. Conversely, should the USD strengthen against EUR,the investor would lose money when converting the EUR back into USD. However, since the forward rate was locked in at the time of the contract, there would be no further loss due to changes in currency values. Use of forward currency contracts requires some knowledge of foreign exchange markets and can be expensive depending on the size of transaction and length of contract. Also, because these contracts involve commitment and future transactions, liquidation or early termination could result in significant costs. So, consult with a professional financial advisor before entering into any forward foreign contract agreement. Invest in companies that generate revenue in multiple geographies Investing in businesses that derive a portion of their revenue from outside their home country can reduce currency exposure relative to their domestic operations. When a company generates sales in several different countries, its revenue isn't quite as exposed to the movement of individual currencies versus the US Dollar. Moreover, selecting firms with diverse global revenue streams can also provide other benefits, like increased product demand, more stable pricing power, and less reliance on a single market or economy. By bond valuation going down, I assume you mean the price of those bonds. If a government's bonds are declining in price, it means market participants expect that the government will have greater difficulty servicing its debt. This may be because they believe the economy is slowing or because there is political uncertainty (such as an impending election) that could affect the ability of the current government to implement sound economic policy.
When bond prices decline, interest rates rise because investors demand higher yields to compensate for the increased risk associated with owning the bonds (in this case, the risk that a default or a devaluation will occur). As a result, governments may need to pay more to entice investors to buy their bonds, which can put pressure on their budget and may force them to consider other options to stabilize their bond market. One option would be for a central bank to purchase the debt, thus artificially increasing the demand and pushing up the prices of these securities. However, this can also lead to inflationary pressures if the money supply increases too much relative to the growth of goods and services, ultimately causing the value of a currency to decline. It can be a delicate balance for governments to maintain the health of their economies while maintaining investor confidence in their debt markets.
